summary: Specifies the ForCES protocol, used between Control Elements and Forwarding Elements inside a network device, which splits the brains of a router from the packet-moving parts. It also states requirements for the Transport Mapping Layer. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ForCES defines how a network device's control functions communicate with its packet-forwarding functions. Control Elements can configure and query Forwarding Elements using a shared set of messages.

questions: control element and forwarding element protocol
what is a control element and forwarding element
what is a logical function block
how does the forces heartbeat work
subtitle: A protocol for control elements to configure and monitor forwarding elements in a network device.

tldr.problem: A network element may separate control functions from packet-forwarding functions. Those parts need a standard way to exchange configuration, queries, events and status.
tldr.mechanism: ForCES uses a master-slave protocol between Control Elements and Forwarding Elements. The protocol layer defines messages, while a separate Transport Mapping Layer carries them and provides transport services.
tldr.outcome: The specification defines association, configuration, query, event, packet redirect and heartbeat messages, as well as transactions and failover behavior. RFC 5810 has been updated by RFC 7121 and RFC 7391.

today: RFC 5810 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7121 and RFC 7391. It has not been obsoleted; it relies on separate TML and FE-model specifications such as RFC 5811 and RFC 5812.

sections.title: Separating Control from Forwarding
sections.content:
Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) standardizes communication between Control Elements (CEs) and Forwarding Elements (FEs) inside a ForCES Network Element. A CE instructs one or more FEs how to process packets; an FE performs per-packet processing using its underlying hardware.

The FE model describes the functions that a CE can control as Logical Function Blocks (LFBs). This protocol carries LFB configuration, capabilities, status and events. It does not define CE-to-CE, FE-to-FE or manager communication.
sections.plainLanguage: A CE decides how packets should be handled, and an FE processes them. ForCES defines the messages they use to coordinate that work.

sections.title: The Protocol Layer and Transport Layer
sections.content:
The ForCES interface has a Protocol Layer (PL) and a Transport Mapping Layer (TML). The PL defines message formats and their meaning. The TML carries PL messages and handles transport concerns such as reliability, ordering, congestion control, security and link availability.

The TML is specified in separate documents, but RFC 5810 lists required services. Implementations of this protocol MUST implement the SCTP-based TML in RFC 5811. CEs and FEs first obtain configuration during pre-association, then exchange protocol messages after association.
sections.plainLanguage: The PL defines the messages; the TML carries them. Before they communicate, the CE and FE obtain the settings they need to associate.

sections.title: The Common Message Header
sections.content:
Every PL message starts with a common header followed by one or more type-length-value (TLV) fields. The header contains a 4-bit version, an 8-bit message type, a 16-bit length measured in 4-byte units, source and destination IDs, a 64-bit correlator and flags.

The correlator lets a CE match a response to its request. The flags include an acknowledgment choice, a priority from 0 to 7, an execution mode and transaction information. The normal priority is 1. TLVs can contain nested TLVs, and older or newer implementations can skip TLV types they do not understand.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the message, its sender and receiver, and the request it answers. The rest of the message uses labeled fields called TLVs.

sections.title: Selecting and Changing LFB Data
sections.content:
A message selects an LFB by its class and instance identifiers. Operations then use a path, a series of component identifiers, to select data within that LFB. Paths can address nested fields or table rows; a key can select a row by its content instead of its index.

ForCES defines operations including SET, SET-PROP, DEL, GET and GET-PROP. FULLDATA carries all components in the order defined by the LFB model; SPARSEDATA carries selected components with identifiers. A zero-length SET does not delete a component; deletion uses DEL.
sections.plainLanguage: A message names an LFB and a path to the data it means to change or read. It can carry all fields or only selected fields.

sections.title: Association, Configuration and Other Messages
sections.content:
An FE starts an association with an Association Setup message, and the CE accepts or rejects it with a response. The CE then configures and queries LFBs. The FE can report subscribed events, and either side can send a heartbeat to indicate liveness.

A Config message can set or delete LFB components and subscribe to events. A Query message requests component values or properties and always expects a response. Packet Redirect messages carry packets or associated metadata between the CE and FE. The FE Object and FE Protocol LFBs expose information about the FE and the protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages let an FE join, receive configuration, answer queries and report events. Heartbeats indicate liveness, while Packet Redirect carries packets or metadata between the elements.

sections.title: Transactions and High Availability
sections.content:
A CE can choose how an FE handles a batch: undo all operations if one fails, continue after failures, or stop at the first failure without undoing earlier work. A transaction spanning several messages can use two-phase commit. FEs first validate the operations; the CE commits only after participating FEs report success.

Only one primary CE controls FEs at a time, though secondary CEs may be configured. On loss of association, one policy returns an FE to pre-association immediately. Another lets it continue forwarding while it tries to reconnect to a primary or secondary CE, until the configured timeout expires.
sections.plainLanguage: For a multi-message change, FEs check whether they can perform each step before the CE commits it. If a CE connection fails, an FE's configured policy determines whether it stops or tries a backup.

sections.title: Security Services and Status
sections.content:
The TML provides security services for the PL. It MUST authenticate CEs and FEs; it SHOULD provide message authentication and confidentiality, using TLS or IPsec as recommended by the RFC. A selected security level applies for the whole session.

Every CE and FE must implement the No Security level, which uses identifier and configuration checks rather than cryptography. The RFC suggests it for endpoints within one box. Operators choose and configure stronger TML security services when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The TML can authenticate the CE and FE and protect messages. The required No Security mode checks configured identities but does not use cryptography.

fields.desc: Upper half of the 64-bit request-response correlator.
